_about: One robot description, two consumers: the TypeScript world builds the body from it, the Java RobotConfig reads the same file.
name: box-v1

chassis._source: guess, sized on a two-pod odometry puck (goBILDA Pinpoint class) rather than measured. WAS ALL ZEROS AND READ BY NOTHING: the brain was handed ground-truth position, heading AND velocity, so the motion lead -- which is built entirely on the reported velocity -- had never been tested against an estimate that could be wrong. vel_mps is the one that matters: a puck differentiates a quantised encoder, and differentiating is the noisiest thing on the robot. 0.04 m/s against a ball horizontal of about 2.3 m/s is one degree of bearing, which is the same order as the launch yaw scatter already modelled. xy_in and heading_deg are a standing error rather than a drift, which flatters a real puck over a long match and is fair over the few seconds a shot takes - CALIBRATE by driving a known square and reading the return error. The TARGET bearing and range are still exact, which is the bigger remaining lie: on a real robot they come from an AprilTag pipeline with its own noise and its own 50-100 ms of latency.

intake.rollerRadius_m_source: guess: a 2.75 in compliant wheel, the usual FTC intake roller - CALIBRATE
intake.rollerMu_source: guess: durometer-35 compliant wheel on a moulded plastic ball. Caps the force the roller can put into a ball - CALIBRATE
intake.squeeze_N_source: guess: how hard the roller is preloaded onto the ball by sitting below ball height. This is the normal load that makes the friction cap non-trivial - CALIBRATE

transfer._source: design parameter - the knob this project exists to explore
transfer.beltRadius_m_source: guess: the drive pulley on the feed belt. Belt speed is motor omega times this, and the belt has to beat gravity to lift a ball up the shaft - CALIBRATE
transfer.indexLift_source: How much of the indexer's push acts upward. A real indexer is a wheel pressed against the ball with its contact patch BELOW the ball's centre, so it lifts as much as it shoves. At 0 -- a purely horizontal shove, which is what this was -- a ball resting on the bin floor is pinned by its own floor contact and does not move at all, so balls only reached the magazine when something else shook them there. Sweep it before trusting the value: the working window measured in the sister build is 0.3-0.8, with 0 and 0.1 feeding nothing and 1.0 throwing balls out of the bin.
transfer.leadLatency_s_source: MEASURED by tools/movingfire.ts --gate. The exit speed is chosen when the gate is commanded and the ball leaves after the feed pulse and the wheel's lag, so under acceleration the shot carries a correction for a velocity the robot has grown out of; leading on v + a*tau predicts the velocity AT RELEASE instead. Deadbanded where a*tau stops being worth more than the flywheel encoder can resolve (one count over a 20 ms window is 107 rpm), because it differentiates a velocity and a standing robot jitters -- applied unconditionally it cost a stationary rig a third of its shots. WAS 0.30, tuned when the lead spent its whole correction on the flywheel and the flywheel therefore lagged badly. The lead solves the hood now, the hood is fast, and there is little stale target left to predict: on the shuttling case 0, 0.15 and 0.30 all land the same 0.36 per second, and 0.30 has the WORST downrange bias of the three (-27 cm against -7 and -5). 0.15 is best or tied on every column, so it is set there, but the honest summary is that this knob no longer moves the answer. Kept because a real feed is slower than this modelled one and a real hood servo will lag in a way this one does not - CALIBRATE tau against a real feed once one exists.

turret._accelSource: guess: 900 deg/s^2 reaches the 180 deg/s slew limit in 0.2 s, which is what a 5203-117 through a 2:1 reduction does against a turret of a few hundred g.cm^2. Derive it properly from motor torque over turret MOI once the real turret exists - CALIBRATE

hood.tolDeg_source: DERIVED from what the wheel is already allowed to be wrong by. The readiness gate accepts flywheel.tolRpm = 60 rpm, which is worth about +-21 cm of range; 1 deg of hood is 3.5 cm of range (tools/fixedspeed.ts), so 60 rpm is about 6 deg of hood and a 2 deg window sits well inside the error already tolerated. It costs almost nothing to wait for -- the lead moves the hood 8.0 deg per m/s of radial speed and the servo does 120 deg/s, so a full-speed run's whole correction arrives in about 0.13 s against a 1.5 s cycle, and tools/movingfire.ts sees this gate close on under 1% of loops. It exists because the motion lead SOLVES the hood: before that the hood only ever held the table's stationary angle and arrived long before the wheel did, so nothing checked it - CALIBRATE against a real servo, which will be slower and may need this loosened.
hood._sweepNote: PLAN.md's default was [30,60]. At that range every solution arrives still CLIMBING at 20-40 deg, threads the mouth and rebounds off the far wall: 19 usable ranges, best speed margin 8.0%. Extending the top of the range to 85 deg lets the ball drop in at 85 deg: 25 usable ranges covering 30-150 in, best margin 14.8% at 75 in. Re-run the sweep if the shooter geometry changes.

flywheel.I_fly_kgm2_source: A 96 mm goBILDA grip wheel (105 g, 1.21e-4 kg.m^2) PLUS a 96 mm x 12 mm 6061 disc behind it: pi*r^2*t*2700 = 234 g, I = 0.5*m*r^2 = 2.70e-4, so 3.91e-4 together and 0.34 kg on the shaft. WAS THE BARE GRIP WHEEL, and no FTC shooter that works is built that way. At 1.21e-4 a single POLLEN takes 210 rpm out of the wheel on its way past (tools/shootercheck.ts), three and a half times the 60 rpm firing window, and the tachometer cannot even see it coming: the hub reports velocity quantised to about 107 rpm a count on a 28-tick encoder, filtered over 6 loops. Every wild shot in tools/_acc.ts was that gap -- fired with the true speed 367 +- 101 rpm under target while the filtered reading said it was fine. Adding inertia is the answer a team reaches for and it costs nothing in the motor budget, which matters here because the robot is already at FTC's 8-motor limit (4 drive, intake, transfer, flywheel, turret) and cannot have a second flywheel motor without giving one up. Spin-up goes from 0.74 s to 2.0 s, which is what a real shooter takes - CALIBRATE by weighing the actual wheel stack.
flywheel._dragSource: guess, sized so windage costs about 5% of stall torque at free speed; a bigger value simply caps the achievable RPM - CALIBRATE from a TuningFlywheel spin-up curve
flywheel._tolRpmSource: the hub velocity loop settles 50-90 RPM above target at these gains, so an 80 RPM window opened only intermittently; 120 RPM is about 3% at the typical 3700 RPM target - tighten it once the loop is calibrated on the real hub
flywheel._source: I_fly from Gecko 96mm (cited); k/lossFactor guesses - CALIBRATE.
flywheel._motorNote: PLAN.md's default was a 5203-1620 at 1:1, which tops out at v_exit = k*w*r = 0.45*169.6*0.048 = 3.7 m/s and cannot reach the HIVE from anywhere on the field. A bare 6000 RPM motor gives 13.6 m/s. A 2:1 step-up on the 1620, or a dual-wheel k of 0.90, would do as well.
flywheel.minLandProb_source: MEASURED, and set by what it COSTS rather than by what it sounds like. The shot is refused unless the robot computes at least this CALIBRATED chance of landing: P(exit speed inside the band that threads the mouth, from the FILTERED wheel speed) x P(pointing inside the mouth, from the current turret error and the launch yaw scatter) x P(a ball arriving like that stays in, from tools/entrycheck.ts), all through the measured curve in config/landcal.json. `npm run tool -- tools/movingfire.ts --sweep` prices it in BALLS PER SECOND, which is the side a per-shot land rate cannot see -- refusing a 60% shot only pays if a better one turns up inside the 1.5 s the refused cycle costs. At 0.70: 0.45 landed per second stopped at 90% of the shots taken, 0.55 closing at 100%, 0.35 shuttling at 100%. 0.80 and above takes the STOPPED case to zero. RE-MEASURE AFTER ANY SHOOTER CHANGE, and do not carry the old number over: it was 0.85 against the bare-grip-wheel flywheel and a noiseless localizer, and both of those moved. It is only meaningful against the landcal curve it was swept on.
flywheel.tolRpm_source: MEASURED by tools/trimsweep.ts against balls in the CELL. It cannot be read off a datasheet because the floor is the encoder: the flywheel runs 28 ticks a rev direct-driven, so the hub's 20 ms velocity window sees 26 counts at 2800 rpm and ONE COUNT is 107 rpm -- about 15 in of range by tools/apercheck.ts. A single reading cannot resolve 30 rpm, which is why rpmFilterFrames exists: six loops of moving average is what makes this window mean anything. 120 rpm is +-14.9 in against a hole 8.9 in deep, and measured worse than 60 at every setting tried.
flywheel.kSkV_source: MEASURED by tools/flywheeltune.ts --ff, which is TuningFlywheel run offline: hold a duty, wait for steady state, record the speed, least-squares fit duty = kS + kV*rpm over 0.2..0.9 duty. Worst residual 0.0037 duty across the range, so the wheel really is that linear. These REPLACE the generic kS = 0.03, kV = 1/freeRpm that genconstants.mjs used to derive: at 2800 rpm the guess asks for 0.497 duty against the measured 0.466, which parks the wheel about 190 rpm high -- far enough outside a 60 rpm readiness window that the robot fires NOTHING. kP is unchanged and only has to cover the dip a shot takes out of the wheel; re-fit all three against a real TuningFlywheel log - CALIBRATE.
flywheel.rpmFilterFrames_source: MEASURED by tools/trimsweep.ts: 1 loop 14.0%, 3 loops 18.3%, 6 loops 31.5% of balls scoring, on the arrival-counting metric that run used. Averaging the hub's velocity estimate costs lag and buys resolution, and one raw reading is quantised to about 107 rpm. FlywheelGate.java carries the same ring buffer so the hub does the same thing.

calibration._about: Field trims. These are what a team actually adjusts between matches: they correct the SHOT TABLE against the real robot without regenerating it, and the Analysis tab computes them from a collected run.
calibration.rangeTrim_in_source: measured: the mean signed downrange error of a collected run. The table is looked up at (range - rangeTrim), so a group landing 8 in LONG gets a trim of +8 and the table is asked for a shorter shot.
calibration.turretTrim_deg_source: measured: atan(mean lateral error / mean range) from a collected run. Subtracted from the commanded azimuth, so it also absorbs a turret encoder zero that is a degree off.

sensors._mountFrame: robot-local FTC convention: x forward, y left, z up (metres)

localizer.velFilterAlpha_source: MEASURED as the smallest filter that keeps the robot shooting once the odometry noise is modelled at all. The lead is built entirely on the reported velocity, so with vel_mps at 0.04 the raw reading jitters the lead azimuth, the turret chases the jitter, its tracking error never settles under the gate's 3 deg and three of the shoot tests fired nothing. One pole at alpha 0.25 on a 60 Hz loop is about 50 ms of lag for roughly a third of the noise. The thing being estimated moves on the timescale of the robot's own acceleration, which is tenths of a second, so 50 ms is cheap - RETUNE against a real puck, whose noise will not be Gaussian.

hub._velocityPidSource: The /32767 scale is the hub's own, which is why f*maxTicksPerSec/32767 is about 1. Measured here on the flywheel settling inside its 80 RPM readiness window 5 s after the command: i=3 lands 186 RPM high, i=8 158 high, i=15 47 high (ready), i=25 20 high. 15 it is - CALIBRATE against a real TuningFlywheel log, and note that a team running its own feedforward + P loop (FlywheelGate) bypasses this entirely.
hub._source: guess - CALIBRATE against TuningDrive logs from a real hub
